snip.t: Post‑renal cascade: obstruction → ↑ hydrostatic pressure proximal to blockage → ↓ net filtration pressure → ↓ GFR → back‑leak of filtrate → hydronephrosis → progressive tubular atrophy if not relieved.

| Obstructive (post‑renal) AKI | Flank pain, palpable bladder, history of stones, prostate enlargement, catheter blockage | Ultrasound shows hydronephrosis; urine output may be normal initially then falls; relief of obstruction rapidly improves GFR. |
Palpable kidneys: Enlarged kidneys can be felt in conditions like polycystic kidney disease or hydronephrosis.
| Urinary Tract Obstruction (Post-renal) | Flank pain, hydronephrosis on imaging | Reversible with relief of obstruction |

qs.q: What is the most common cause of hydronephrosis in infants and children?
qs.e: UPJ obstruction is the most common cause of hydronephrosis in infants and children. Prostatic hyperplasia is a common cause of bilateral distal obstruction in older men rather than in infants.
qs.s: Disorders of the lower urinary tract — revision: MCQs

qs.q: Which portion of the nephron fails first functionally during the development of hydronephrosis?
o: Distal tubules fail last due to regional hyperperfusion
Loop of Henle fails first due to primary ureteral dilation
Tubules fail first due to medullary blood flow compression
Glomeruli fail first due to immediate cortical ischemia
qs.e: Tubules fail first because medullary vessels are compressed early, compromising the blood flow required for urinary concentration. GFR falls later as the cortex atrophies.
qs.s: Urinary Tract Obstruction & Hydronephrosis: Causes, Symptoms: MCQs

qs.q: What is the investigation of choice for initially diagnosing hydronephrosis in a patient with suspected urinary obstruction?
qs.e: Ultrasonography is the non-invasive investigation of choice that readily demonstrates a dilated renal pelvis and calyces. Plain X-rays miss radiolucent stones and soft tissue obstruction details.
qs.s: Urinary Tract Obstruction & Hydronephrosis: Causes, Symptoms: MCQs

qs.q: What pathological finding characterizes the chronic stage of hydronephrosis morphology?
o: Massive proliferation of normal medullary renal pyramids
Cortical tubular atrophy and diffuse interstitial fibrosis
Hypertrophy of the renal glomeruli with increased GFR
Immediate conversion of the kidney into an alkaline cyst
qs.e: Chronic hydronephrosis is characterized by cortical tubular atrophy, diffuse interstitial fibrosis, and blunting of the pyramid apices. Glomerular filtration and cortical thickness actually decrease over time.
qs.s: Urinary Tract Obstruction & Hydronephrosis: Causes, Symptoms: MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man presents with bilateral hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
qs.e: Bilateral obstruction is typically caused by distal lesions such as prostatic hyperplasia, whereas unilateral obstruction is more often due to proximal causes like stones or UPJ obstruction.
qs.s: Lower Urinary Tract & Ureter Pathology: Obstruction & Tumors: MCQs

qs.q: A child presents with unilateral hydronephrosis. Which congenital anomaly is the most common cause in this age group?
qs.e: UPJ obstruction is the most common cause of hydronephrosis in infants and children, while vesicoureteral reflux primarily predisposes to pyelonephritis.
qs.s: Lower Urinary Tract & Ureter Pathology: Obstruction & Tumors: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old man is found to have unilateral hydronephrosis caused by compression of the mid-ureter by an abnormal pathological process originating outside the urinary tract. Which condition represents an extrinsic cause of ureteral obstruction?
qs.e: Retroperitoneal fibrosis causes extrinsic compression and encasement of the ureters, whereas strictures, calculi, and clots represent intrinsic luminal obstructions. Intrinsic stones originate inside the lumen, whereas retroperitoneal fibrosis exerts pressure from the surrounding anatomical space.
qs.s: Lower Urinary Tract & Ureter Pathology: Obstruction & Tumors: MCQs

qs.q: A renal ultrasound is performed on a neonate with antenatal hydronephrosis. Which ultrasonographic finding distinguishes a ureteropelvic junction obstruction from a ureterovesical junction obstruction?
qs.e: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction classically demonstrates isolated renal pelvis dilation without downstream ureteral enlargement, whereas ureterovesical obstruction involves dilation of both the pelvis and the ureter. Bilateral calyceal cysts suggest cystic dysplasia rather than simple mechanical outflow obstruction.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Hydronephrosis is the dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces caused by urine back‑pressure from an obstruction, leading to progressive kidney damage if untreated.

sections.p: Hydronephrosis is the swelling of the kidney’s collecting system due to impaired urine flow. Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging, usually ultrasound, which shows calyceal dilatation and loss of cortical thickness.

t.b: Shows dilated pelvis/calyces and cortical thinning – confirms obstruction and estimates severity
Provides detailed anatomy of obstruction site and any stones or masses – used when ultrasound is inconclusive

sections.p: Staging follows the Society of Urologic Surgeons system: Stage I (mild dilatation, preserved function) to Stage IV (severe dilatation, loss of function).
b: Stage IV: >3 cm dilatation, GFR <30 ml/min

sections.p: Obstruction can be intrinsic or extrinsic. In low‑resource settings, common causes include stones, infections, and pregnancy‑related changes.
b: Infections such as schistosomiasis – can cause bladder wall thickening

sections.p: Symptoms vary with severity and side. Mild cases may be asymptomatic; severe cases cause flank pain, hematuria, fever, or oliguria.
b: Reduced urine output – in bilateral obstruction

sections.p: Work‑up focuses on confirming obstruction, identifying cause, and assessing kidney function.
b: Cystoscopy – if bladder outlet obstruction suspected

t.b: Elevated creatinine indicates impaired filtration – higher values suggest more severe obstruction
Declining eGFR signals progressive loss of renal function – guides urgency of intervention

sections.p: Urgent care is needed if there is infection, loss of kidney function, or impending renal failure.
b: Severe bilateral hydronephrosis – can cause oligohydramnios in pregnancy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve obstruction, and protect remaining renal function. Supportive care includes hydration and infection control.
b: Avoid nephrotoxic drugs – to preserve remaining function

sections.p: Regular imaging and renal function tests are essential. Prevention focuses on early stone treatment and infection control.
b: Treat UTIs promptly to avoid obstruction

sections.p: Conditions that mimic hydronephrosis include renal cysts, pyelonephritis, and abdominal masses.
b: Abdominal mass – may compress ureter but not dilate pelvis

sections.p: Normal ultrasound can miss early obstruction; creatinine may remain normal until significant loss of function.
b: Creatinine – can stay within normal limits until >50% loss of function

faq.q: What is the most common cause worldwide?
faq.a: Kidney stones are the leading cause of urinary obstruction leading to hydronephrosis.
Adequate fluid intake can help flush small stones but does not relieve established obstruction.
